definition: In computer software development, genetic improvement is the use of optimisation and machine learning techniques, particularly search-based software engineering techniques such as genetic programming to improve existing software.
details: The improved program need not behave identically to the original. For example, automatic bug fixing improves executable code by reducing or eliminating buggy behaviour. In other cases the improved software should behave identically to the old version but is better because, for example: it runs faster, it uses less memory, it uses less energy or it runs on a different type of computer. GI differs from, for example, formal program translation, in that it primarily verifies the behaviour of the new mutant version by running both the new and the old software on test inputs and comparing their output and performance in order to see if the new software can still do what is wanted of the original program and is now better. Genetic improvement can be used to create multiple versions of programs, each tailored to be better for a particular use or for a particular computer. Genetic improvement can be used with multi-objective optimization to consider improving software along multiple dimensions or to consider trade-offs between several objectives, such as asking GI to evolve programs which trade speed against the quality of answers they give. Of course it may be possible to find programs which are both faster and give better answers. Mostly, genetic improvement makes typically small changes or edits (also known as mutations) to the program's source code but sometimes the mutations are made to assembly code, byte code or binary machine code.

explainer.lead: Genetic improvement automatically edits existing software and tests the variants to find one that works better. It can fix bugs or improve speed, memory use, energy use, and hardware compatibility without requiring developers to make every change by hand.

tiers.eli5: Imagine making small changes to a recipe, then tasting each version to see whether it is still good and perhaps quicker to make. Genetic improvement does something similar with computer programs: it tries little edits, tests the results, and keeps the versions that work better.
tiers.practitioner: Apply genetic programming or other search-based software engineering techniques to generate small mutations, then run both original and modified programs on test inputs and compare their outputs and performance. Mutations may target source code, assembly, bytecode, or binary machine code, and multi-objective search can balance goals such as speed and answer quality. Passing tests does not formally prove that the new program preserves the required behaviour, so test coverage matters.
tiers.paperLevel: Given an original program P and test inputs T, GI searches a space of mutated programs P' and evaluates each candidate by comparing P and P' on T for behaviour and performance. Optimization may use several objectives, such as minimizing runtime while maximizing answer quality, and can produce variants tailored to particular uses or computers. Behavioural equivalence is primarily established empirically by testing rather than by formal translation or proof.

explainer.example: A program gives correct answers but runs too slowly. Genetic improvement produces small code mutations, checks each variant against the original on test inputs, and retains a version that still gives the wanted answers while running faster.

usedIn.name: Automatic bug fixing
usedIn.detail: Edits executable code to reduce or eliminate buggy behaviour.

usedIn.name: Software performance optimization
usedIn.detail: Searches for variants that run faster or use less memory while retaining the desired behaviour.

usedIn.name: Energy-aware software
usedIn.detail: Improves programs so that they consume less energy.

usedIn.name: Hardware-specific software
usedIn.detail: Creates program versions tailored to particular uses or different types of computers.

explainer.intuition: Treat an existing program as the starting point for an evolutionary search rather than writing its replacement from scratch. Repeatedly mutate it, test whether each variant still does what is wanted, and favour variants that perform better.
howItWorks: Start with an existing program and decide what should improve, such as correctness, speed, memory, or energy use.
Make typically small edits to its source code, or sometimes to assembly, bytecode, or binary machine code.
Run the original and mutant programs on test inputs and compare their outputs and performance.
Keep promising variants and continue searching until a sufficiently improved version is found.
Optionally optimize several objectives together to explore trade-offs such as speed versus answer quality.
explainer.whyItMatters: It can improve software that already exists instead of requiring a complete rewrite. The same search process can also generate multiple versions suited to different uses, computers, or performance trade-offs.
misconceptions: The improved program does not always have to behave identically; automatic bug fixing intentionally changes buggy behaviour.
GI is not formal program translation: it mainly checks candidate behaviour by running tests and comparing results.
It is not limited to source code, because mutations can also target assembly, bytecode, or binary machine code.
